title: BESSIE VS. THE ALGORITHM
hook: The world tour has a time limit.
beats: Welcome to the farm tour

Bessie has one dream: headline the biggest music festival in the pasture. Unfortunately, her manager is a cow named T L E: Time Limit Exceeded. He booked two hundred thousand fans, then checked every possible pair to decide who gets matching friendship bracelets. Forty billion checks later, the concert is over. The grass has retired. Your mission is to replace this management team with algorithms.
Your four campaign worlds

We will build from C plus plus basics to Bronze problem solving, Silver techniques, Gold algorithms, and a Platinum extension. These are learning groups, not an official fixed syllabus. Problems mix ideas, and division boundaries move. You do not need advanced trees to start Bronze. You need careful reading, correct code, and the confidence to test an idea instead of staring at it like it owes you money.
Watching is the tutorial. Coding is the game.

This is a long film with chapters. Watch in short sessions. When a challenge appears, pause and write code before the answer. Keep a notebook of wrong assumptions and useful patterns. One film cannot teach every possible contest trick or replace months of practice. It can give you a coherent map, worked examples, and a way to learn the next thing. Welcome to the training arc. Your compiler has absolutely no plot armor.
challenge: Create a folder and a notebook. Write your current experience and a first goal.
answer: A useful first goal: compile a program, read numbers, and explain its output.

title: C++: THE FIRST SOUND CHECK
hook: Semicolons: tiny, expensive commas.
beats: Source -> compiler -> executable

A program is a precise set of instructions. You write source code in a dot C P P file. A compiler checks it and builds an executable. Running that executable performs the instructions. Use a local editor and compiler, or a suitable online C plus plus environment. For this course the examples use C plus plus seventeen. Check the contest rules for the compiler versions accepted when you compete.
Read, compute, print

The include lines make library features available. Main is where execution begins. C in reads input, C out prints output. The arrow direction is a memory aid: input flows toward your variables; output flows toward the screen. The program shown reads two integers and prints their sum. Input three and four produces seven. It does not produce a motivational quote. Judges are extremely difficult audiences.
Compiler errors are coordinates

Compile with g plus plus, the C plus plus seventeen flag, warnings, and an output name. Then run the executable with sample input. Fix the first meaningful compiler error before chasing the rest; one missing brace can generate a whole diss track. A compile error means no executable was successfully built. A wrong answer means it ran but did the wrong thing. These are different problems and need different debugging moves.
challenge: Compile this program. Try 3 4, -5 8, and 0 0.
answer: 7, 3, and 0. Command: g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra main.cpp -o main

title: VARIABLES HAVE A STORAGE LIMIT
hook: Overflow is not a remix.
beats: Names, values, types

A variable is a named storage location with a type. Int stores whole numbers; long long stores larger whole numbers; double stores approximate real numbers. Bool stores true or false. Char stores one character, and string stores text. Initialize your variables before reading them. An uninitialized local integer is not a surprise feature. It is a bug wearing a mystery box costume.
Promotion must happen BEFORE multiplication

A typical thirty two bit signed int tops out near two point one billion. One hundred thousand times one hundred thousand is ten billion. Even if you assign the result to long long, multiplying two ints first can overflow. Write one L L times a times b, or make an operand long long. Signed overflow is undefined behavior in C plus plus, not a dependable wraparound shortcut.
Integer division and modulo

Seven divided by two using integers is three. Seven modulo two is one. For a real quotient, convert an operand to double. For nonnegative integers and positive b, ceiling division can be written a over b plus whether a modulo b is nonzero; this avoids the addition overflow risk in a plus b minus one. Negative numbers need more care. Types are part of the algorithm, not decorative accessories.
challenge: What does 5 / 2 print? How do you obtain 2.5?
answer: Integer operands produce 2. Use 5.0 / 2 or double(5) / 2.

title: IF STATEMENTS AND THE LOOP TOUR
hook: The NPC finally gets instructions.
beats: Branches are decisions

An if statement runs code when a condition is true. Else handles the other case. Double equals compares; a single equals assigns. And requires both conditions; or requires at least one. Put braces around blocks while learning. If Bessie has a ticket and the gate is open, let her in. If she merely claims to know the DJ, that is not a boolean credential.
Loops repeat a controlled job

A for loop often has initialization, a condition, and an update. Start i at zero, continue while i is less than n, increment i. That visits zero through n minus one exactly once. A while loop repeats while its condition holds. Make sure something changes toward termination. Otherwise you have built an infinite livestream with no subscribers and a very warm laptop.
Trace before you trust

Suppose the values are two, five, and three. Start sum at zero. After each visit, the running totals are two, seven, and ten. A loop invariant is a statement true before and after each iteration. Here, sum equals the total of all values already processed. This simple idea grows into formal correctness proofs. Trace small inputs by hand: it is the debugging equivalent of checking your microphone before the show.
challenge: For input values -2, 5, 0, 3, what sum does this loop keep?
answer: 8: only strictly positive values contribute.

title: ARRAYS, VECTORS, AND STRINGS
hook: Index zero has entered the chat.
beats: Contiguous values, explicit indices

A vector is a resizable sequence. Vector of int, a of n, creates n integers initialized to zero. The first index is zero; the last is n minus one. Index n is outside the vector. C plus plus does not promise a friendly error if you go out of bounds. Push back appends a value. Size reports the number of elements, not the final valid index.
Strings are sequences too

A string behaves like a sequence of characters. C in reads one whitespace-separated token. Getline reads a whole line, which matters for text containing spaces. After formatted input, handle the leftover newline before getline. To count letters, loop over characters and update frequencies. Be explicit about the expected alphabet; indexing by character minus lowercase a only makes sense for lowercase English letters.
References avoid surprise copies

A range loop with auto x copies each element. Auto ampersand x refers to the actual element, so assigning changes the vector. Const auto ampersand avoids copying while preventing modification. For a two dimensional grid, use a vector of vectors or another suitable representation. Always check both row and column boundaries. Negative one is not the secret bonus row.
challenge: Why is a[a.size()] invalid for a nonempty vector?
answer: Indices end at size minus one; size itself is one past the end.

title: FUNCTIONS, PAIRS, AND THE TOOLBOX
hook: Your code needs a crew.
beats: Functions have contracts

A function takes parameters, does a job, and may return a value. Give it a contract: what inputs it accepts, what output it promises, and what it changes. Passing a large vector by value copies it. Pass by const reference when you only need to inspect it. Pass by mutable reference when changing the original is intentional. Name functions after the job, not your current emotional state.
Useful standard containers

A pair groups two values. A struct gives related fields meaningful names. Vector stores sequences. Set stores distinct ordered keys. Map associates ordered keys with values. Queue removes the earliest inserted item; stack removes the latest. Priority queue retrieves the highest priority item, a maximum by default. Unordered containers offer average constant time lookup but have worst cases. Choose based on operations, not the coolest sounding name.
Learn the operations, not the entire manual

Sort rearranges a range. Lower bound searches an ordered range. Min and max compare values. Accumulate adds a range; its initial value determines the accumulation type, so use zero L L for long long sums. Include the appropriate standard headers. Contest code often uses a GCC convenience header, but it is not standard C plus plus. Our companion examples use explicit headers so the dependencies are visible.
challenge: Choose containers: FIFO line, unique sorted IDs, and next cheapest task.
answer: queue, set, and a min-heap priority_queue respectively.

title: BIG O: THE BOUNCER OF RUNTIME
hook: Forty billion checks are not a vibe.
beats: Count growth, not exact seconds

Big O describes how resource use grows as input grows. One pass is linear. Two nested full passes are quadratic. Repeated halving is logarithmic. Sorting is commonly n log n. Drop constant factors when naming the growth rate, but remember constants and memory still matter in practice. There is no universal operations-per-second guarantee. Use limits, an operation estimate, and measurements when necessary.
Constraints choose the neighborhood

With n around twenty, enumerating subsets may fit. Around one thousand, some quadratic algorithms may fit. Around two hundred thousand, you usually seek near-linear or n log n approaches. These are rough clues, not permissions. Two to the n and n factorial grow explosively. A factorial algorithm for a large concert lineup is basically asking the heat death of the universe to open for Bessie.
Memory is also a budget

An n by n table for two hundred thousand items is impossible in ordinary contest memory. Estimate element count times bytes, then include container overhead. Recursive depth also uses stack memory. Ask both how many states exist and how often each is processed. A beautiful recurrence can still exceed time or memory. T L E and Memory Limit Exceeded are cousins; neither is invited backstage.
challenge: For n = 200000, estimate n squared and compare with about n log2 n.
answer: 40 billion versus roughly 3.6 million; constants differ, but growth strongly favors the latter.

title: SIMULATION: READ THE FINE PRINT
hook: The problem statement is the contract.
beats: Represent the state

Simulation follows the stated process directly. Write down the state: positions, capacities, balances, directions, or time. Then define exactly what one operation does. In a bucket transfer, move the minimum of the source amount and destination free space. Subtract from one bucket and add to the other. Conservation of total milk becomes an invariant you can test after every move.
Order changes answers

Suppose bucket A has seven units with capacity ten, and bucket B has four with capacity five. Transfer from A to B: only one unit moves. The new amounts are six and five. Computing free space after accidentally modifying B can give the wrong result. Save intermediate quantities when updates depend on the old state. An algorithm is a choreography; doing the moonwalk in the wrong direction still moves you somewhere.
Build a tiny oracle

For a simple simulation, implement the literal process first. Test zero capacity if allowed, a full destination, an empty source, and repeated operations. When a problem asks for an enormous number of steps, look for cycles or a mathematical shortcut, but prove the shortcut matches the process. Do not optimize a misunderstood rule. That is just making wrong answers arrive with premium shipping.
challenge: A has 8, B has 2, and B capacity is 6. Transfer A to B.
answer: Move 4; A becomes 4 and B becomes 6.

title: BRUTE FORCE IS A VALID OPENING ACT
hook: Small constraints? Take the free points.
beats: Enumerate all valid candidates

Brute force tries every candidate when the search space is small enough. To find the best pair, loop i from zero to n minus one, and j from i plus one onward. This avoids pairing an item with itself and avoids duplicate unordered pairs. Score each pair and keep the best. The correctness argument is that every valid pair appears exactly once.
Subsets and permutations

A subset can be represented by a bit mask when n is small. Bit i tells whether item i is selected. There are two to the n masks. Permutations represent orderings, and there are n factorial of them. Start a permutation enumeration from sorted order when using next permutation to list all distinct arrangements. An exponential method is not automatically bad; it is bad when the actual limits make it too large.
Pruning requires a reason

Backtracking builds a candidate gradually and abandons branches that cannot lead to a valid or better answer. Prune only when you have a logical guarantee. A partial score that looks disappointing may later improve. Keep a slow, obviously correct solver for small inputs even after building a fast one. Comparing the two on random tiny cases catches bugs faster than staring at a function named definitely correct final version three.
challenge: How many unordered distinct pairs exist among five items?

title: SORTING AND THE COMPARATOR COURT
hook: A comparator cannot say everyone wins.
beats: Order reveals structure

Sorting puts related values together. This enables adjacent comparisons, grouping duplicates, greedy choices, and two pointers. C plus plus sort on a vector of n items takes order n log n comparisons. Sort pairs lexicographically by default: first component, then second. For custom behavior, define a comparator that returns true only when the first item should come strictly before the second.
Strict means strict

Do not use less than or equal as a sort comparator. Comparing an item with itself must return false. Your comparator also needs consistent transitive ordering. For events, choose a clear tie rule. Sorting by finish time and then start time is a valid choice. If you need to preserve original order among equal keys, use stable sort or carry an original index and choose a deliberate rule.
Sorting changes positions

If the problem cares about original indices, store each value together with its index before sorting. After sorting, neighboring values are neighboring in value order, not necessarily in the original input. This distinction matters for tasks about adjacent physical cows. Sorting a line of cows by coolness and then pretending nobody moved is how your algorithm gets sued by the seating chart.
challenge: Why is return a <= b an invalid comparator for sort?
answer: It says a comes before itself, violating strict weak ordering.

title: BRONZE BOSS: THE FESTIVAL AUDIT
hook: No plot armor. Just test cases.
beats: A complete solving workflow

Read the task once for the story and again for the mathematical specification. Identify inputs, outputs, limits, and edge cases. Work through a tiny example by hand. Describe an algorithm in plain language. Explain why it covers every valid possibility. Estimate time and memory. Then code. This order feels slower for the first five minutes and saves the next forty minutes of debugging interpretive dance.
Bounding boxes and intervals

For axis-aligned rectangles, overlap width is max of zero and minimum right edge minus maximum left edge. Height is analogous. Multiply using a sufficiently wide type. For integer grid points, endpoint conventions may change the count; geometric length and number of integer positions are not identical. Draw a picture and label whether boundaries count. Off-by-one bugs love pretending to be geometry.
Your first gate

Pause for a mini project: read n ticket prices, print the sum, the maximum, and the number of distinct prices. A simple sorted-vector solution is enough. Test one price, all equal prices, and a mixture with duplicates. Explain the runtime. If this still feels hard, stay here and practice. Bronze is not embarrassing; skipping fundamentals and then fighting a segment tree with a spoon is embarrassing.
challenge: Prices: 4, 2, 4, 9, 2. Find sum, maximum, distinct count.
answer: 21, 9, 3. Sort then count changes; O(n log n) time.

title: PREFIX SUMS: MIX ONCE, SAMPLE OFTEN
hook: Stop replaying the whole album.
beats: Store totals of prefixes

Suppose ticket sales are three, one, four, one, five. Make a prefix array of length n plus one. Prefix zero is zero. Prefix i plus one equals prefix i plus the value at i. The resulting totals are zero, three, four, eight, nine, fourteen. Each entry summarizes everything before its index. Like an album timestamp, it lets you jump directly to the part you want.
Subtract the part you do not need

Use half-open ranges: left is included, right is excluded. The sum on left through right is prefix right minus prefix left. For indices one through four, subtract prefix one from prefix four: nine minus three equals six. That includes values one, four, one. Preprocessing takes linear time, each query constant time, and storage linear space. Use long long if accumulated totals can exceed int.
Why subtraction works

Prefix right contains the desired range plus everything before left. Prefix left contains exactly that unwanted earlier part. Subtraction cancels it. This proof also tells you the limitation: if values change frequently, these stored prefixes become stale. Prefix sums are excellent for static sum queries, but not automatically for dynamic updates. A cached answer from yesterday is not clairvoyance.
challenge: On [3,1,4,1,5], find the sum of [2,5).

title: DIFFERENCE ARRAYS AND 2D PREFIXES
hook: A guest verse at the boundaries.
beats: Range additions become two events

Suppose many operations add x to every position in a half-open interval. Update difference left by plus x and difference right by minus x. After all operations, take a running sum to reconstruct the additions at each position. The positive event starts the effect; the negative event stops it. Allocate n plus one slots so a stop at n is safe. This is efficient when updates can be collected before answers are needed.
A rectangle has four corners

A two dimensional prefix table stores the sum above and to the left of a boundary. To query a rectangle, take the big prefix, subtract the two unwanted strips, and add their overlap back because it was subtracted twice. Draw the four regions rather than memorizing a mysterious spell. Inclusion and exclusion is just careful bookkeeping wearing a wizard cape.
Know what the table costs

A grid with r rows and c columns takes order r times c memory for a full prefix table. That is fine for some grids and impossible for huge coordinates. Coordinate compression can preserve order, but does not automatically preserve physical distances. For sparse geometry, a sweep line may be more appropriate. Choose a representation based on actual occupied data and the queries, not the size of the fictional pasture.

title: TWO POINTERS: THE COLLAB THAT MOVES
hook: Two features. One linear scan.
beats: Sorted two-sum

Given a sorted array and a target, put one pointer at each end. If their sum is too small, move the left pointer right. If too large, move the right pointer left. If equal, you found a pair. Why is discarding safe? With the right value fixed, a too-small left value cannot work with any smaller right value either. Sorting creates the monotonic structure that justifies the movement.
Every pointer has a movement budget

For values one, two, four, seven, eleven and target nine, one plus eleven is too large, so reduce the right end. One plus seven is too small, so advance the left end. Two plus seven is nine. Each pointer moves at most n times; the scan is linear after sorting. Nested-looking loops can still be linear if the total movement is bounded.
Sliding windows need a valid invariant

For nonnegative values, a window sum increases when you extend right and decreases when you remove left. This supports finding the longest window with sum at most a limit. Negative values destroy that monotonic behavior, so the same procedure may fail. Do not use two pointers just because you own two fingers. First explain why moving one boundary can safely discard candidates.
challenge: Why must the simple sum-limited sliding window assume nonnegative values?
answer: With negatives, extending can reduce a sum and removing can increase it; the usual discard argument fails.

title: BINARY SEARCH: DELETE HALF THE DRAMA
hook: The answer is hiding in a monotone crowd.
beats: Search a sorted range

Binary search repeatedly halves an ordered search interval. Lower bound returns the first element not less than a target. Upper bound returns the first element greater than it. Their iterator difference counts occurrences in a sorted vector. If no matching boundary exists, an iterator can equal end; do not dereference it. End is an exit sign, not another seat.
Search answers, not just arrays

Suppose a truck capacity is feasible if all packages can ship within a fixed number of days. A larger capacity is also feasible. This gives a false region followed by a true region. Search for the first true capacity, using a greedy feasibility check that fills each day in order. Establish a feasible upper bound and a lower bound; for nonnegative weights, maximum weight and total weight are natural bounds.
Maintain an explicit invariant

With an inclusive interval containing the first feasible answer, choose mid as low plus half of high minus low. If mid works, set high to mid; otherwise set low to mid plus one. Stop when low equals high. The predicate must be monotone and the bounds must contain a feasible answer. If each check is linear, total time is n times log of the answer range, not just log n.
challenge: Truth values are F,F,F,T,T,T at indices 0..5. What boundary is found?
answer: 3. Without the false-then-true property, this algorithm is not justified.

title: GREEDY: CONFIDENCE NEEDS A PROOF
hook: Main-character energy is not correctness.
beats: A locally best choice

A greedy algorithm commits to a choice and does not reconsider it. For selecting the maximum number of non-overlapping shows, sort by finishing time. Repeatedly take the earliest-finishing compatible show. Use a clear convention: if intervals are half-open, a show starting exactly when another ends is compatible. The choice preserves as much remaining time as possible.
Exchange argument

Take an optimal schedule. Its first show cannot end earlier than the earliest-finishing available show. Replace that first show with our choice. Every later show in the optimal schedule still fits, so the number selected does not decrease. Repeat on the remaining suffix. This is an exchange argument. We did not prove it by saying the choice feels efficient while a bass drop distracts the reviewer.
A counterexample ends the argument

Choosing the shortest show first can fail. A short interval in the middle may block two compatible longer intervals, one on either side. Greedy also fails for some coin systems: coins one, three, four and target six. Taking four first needs three coins, while three plus three needs two. Before coding a greedy rule, hunt for a tiny counterexample. One counterexample defeats a thousand successful random examples.
challenge: With coins 1,3,4 and target 6, compare largest-first with optimal.
answer: Largest-first uses 4+1+1: three coins. Optimal uses 3+3: two.

title: SETS, MAPS, AND COORDINATE COMPRESSION
hook: Huge numbers, small guest list.
beats: Ordered lookup

An ordered set supports insertion, deletion, and finding a lower bound in logarithmic time. A multiset permits duplicates. Erasing by value from a multiset can remove all equivalent values; erasing a specific iterator removes just that one element. Check whether an iterator is valid before using it. In a ticket allocation problem, the previous element before upper bound can give the largest affordable remaining ticket.
Counting and grouping

A map can count frequencies or associate each identifier with a state. Access with square brackets can insert a missing key with a default value. Use find when you only want to test existence without insertion. Unordered maps have useful average complexity but do not keep sorted order and are not guaranteed constant time in the worst case. Do not rely on their iteration order for deterministic logic.
Compress ranks, preserve distances separately

If coordinates are enormous but there are only n of them, sort and deduplicate the coordinates, then replace each with its rank. This preserves less-than and equality relations. It does not preserve gaps: coordinates ten and one billion become neighboring ranks even though they are far apart. Keep the original coordinate array when lengths or areas matter. Compression is a seating chart, not a shrink ray for geography.
challenge: Compress [100, 7, 100, 50] using zero-based sorted ranks.
answer: Unique sorted coordinates [7,50,100]; ranks [2,0,2,1].

title: GRAPHS: THE FESTIVAL GROUP CHAT
hook: Friendships are edges. Drama is optional.
beats: Vertices and edges

A graph consists of vertices and edges. Vertices can represent cows, rooms, or states. Edges represent allowed relationships or moves. Edges may be directed or undirected and may have weights. An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbors. For an undirected edge, add both directions. An adjacency matrix uses quadratic memory, so it is usually unsuitable for a large sparse graph.
DFS explores deeply

Depth first search follows a path until it cannot continue, then backtracks. Mark a vertex visited when you discover it, so cycles do not cause infinite recursion. Start a search from each unvisited vertex to count connected components. Each vertex is processed once and each adjacency entry is examined once: linear time in vertices plus edges. A long chain can overflow the call stack, so an explicit stack is safer for deep graphs.
State must match the question

If being at a room with a key differs from being there without a key, those are different states. Marking only the room visited would lose information. A useful graph model captures every piece of history that changes future possibilities. Too little state gives wrong answers; too much state explodes memory. This balance reappears in dynamic programming. Your state is the plot summary the future actually needs.
challenge: An undirected graph has edges 0-1, 1-2, and 3-4. How many components?
answer: 2, assuming the vertices are exactly 0 through 4.

title: BFS AND FLOOD FILL
hook: The queue has a fair admissions policy.
beats: Layers give shortest unweighted paths

Breadth first search uses a first-in-first-out queue. Start with the source at distance zero. When you discover an unvisited neighbor, assign distance current plus one and enqueue it. Mark it immediately, not later when it leaves the queue. Vertices are processed by nondecreasing distance, so the first discovery gives a shortest path when every edge has equal cost.
Grids are graphs in disguise

In a grid, each open cell is a vertex and valid neighboring moves are edges. Check row and column boundaries before reading a cell. Flood fill counts connected regions or measures their sizes. Four-directional movement and eight-directional movement produce different graphs. Read the statement. Diagonal movement is not a free DLC that you can install because the level feels difficult.
Recover paths and combine sources

Store a parent when discovering a vertex to reconstruct one shortest path. For distance to the nearest of several sources, initialize all sources at distance zero and put them all in the queue. This is multi-source breadth first search. If edges have arbitrary unequal weights, ordinary BFS no longer guarantees shortest cost; use the right weighted algorithm later in the film.
challenge: Why does BFS mark a node when enqueuing it?
answer: To prevent duplicate discoveries and preserve the first, shortest unweighted distance.

title: TREES, PARENTS, AND SUBTREES
hook: One connected graph. Zero cycles. Peace.
beats: The unique-path property

A tree is a connected undirected graph without cycles. With n vertices it has n minus one edges, and there is exactly one simple path between any two vertices. Choose a root to define parents, children, depths, and subtrees. The root is a viewpoint, not a special physical property of the original graph. Changing it changes the family tree, not the roads.
Compute after the children

To compute subtree sizes, initialize each size to one. Visit each child, compute its subtree size, and add that result to the parent. This is a postorder computation: a parent depends on completed child results. For large trees, an iterative traversal can build an order, then processing the reversed order handles children first. Avoid assuming the system stack can hold two hundred thousand recursive calls.
Diameter and caution

In an unweighted tree, a search from any vertex finds a farthest vertex; a second search from that farthest vertex finds a diameter endpoint and its distance. The diameter is a longest shortest path. This two-search fact relies on tree structure; it is not a universal recipe for arbitrary graphs. When a technique works brilliantly in one setting, write down its assumptions before promoting it to a lifestyle.
challenge: Root a chain 0-1-2-3 at 0. What are subtree sizes?

title: SILVER BOSS: COORDINATE THE TOUR
hook: Choose the pattern from evidence.
beats: Three clues, three tools

Many static range sums suggest prefix sums. A maximum or minimum feasible answer with a monotone yes-or-no test suggests binary search on the answer. Reachability among relationships suggests a graph traversal. These are clues, not automatic labels. Translate the story into operations, constraints, and invariants before choosing the tool. The cows may wear different costumes, but the mathematical job is what matters.
Worked capacity check

Packages have weights three, two, two, four, one, four, in that order. With capacity six, the days are three plus two, then two plus four, then one plus four: three days. With capacity five, four days are needed. If the goal is three days, six is feasible and five is not. Larger capacities remain feasible because you can keep the same grouping.
Your promotion test

Implement this shipping problem with binary search and a linear greedy check. Compare against trying every capacity on small random positive arrays. Also solve a connected-components problem and a static range-sum problem from scratch. Explain the proof and complexity aloud. When you can do that without peeking, you own the idea. If you only recognize the code, you have attended the concert but have not learned the instrument.
challenge: For [3,2,2,4,1,4] and at most 3 days, find minimum capacity.
answer: 6. A capacity of 5 requires 4 days; 6 works in 3.

title: DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING: REMEMBER THE REMIX
hook: Stop solving the same problem twelve times.
beats: A state is a precise question

Dynamic programming reuses solutions to overlapping subproblems. Start by defining a state in one sentence. For minimum coins, D P of s is the fewest coins needed to make total s. Set D P of zero to zero and other states to an unreachable sentinel. For each total, consider a final coin and use the previously solved smaller total. The recurrence follows from asking what the final decision could have been.
Transition, base, order, answer

With coins one, three, and four, the totals zero through six need zero, one, two, one, one, two, and two coins. To compute total six, consider the answer for five plus a one coin, three plus a three coin, or two plus a four coin. The best is two. Write four things before coding: the state meaning, transitions, base cases, and evaluation order. Then identify where the final answer lives.
Prove both directions

Every transition must construct a valid solution, and every optimal solution must be represented by some transition. Here, removing the last coin from an optimal solution leaves a smaller valid total. If that remainder were not solved optimally, replacing it would improve the whole solution. This is optimal substructure. Memorizing a formula without a state definition is like sampling a song without knowing where the beat starts.
challenge: Using coins 2 and 5, which totals 0 through 7 are unreachable?
answer: 1 and 3. Never add to an unreachable sentinel without checking it.

title: KNAPSACK: THE MERCH BAG HAS LIMITS
hook: You cannot pack the entire gift shop.
beats: Choose each item at most once

In zero-one knapsack, each item has a weight and value, and may be taken once. Define D P of i and capacity as the best value using the first i items within that capacity. Either skip the next item or take it if it fits. This produces order n times capacity time. That is pseudo-polynomial: it depends on the numeric capacity, which may be enormous even when its written representation is short.
Why the loop goes backward

We can compress away the item dimension. For each item, iterate capacities downward. This ensures the source state comes from before the current item was used. Iterating upward can reuse the same item repeatedly, accidentally solving an unbounded knapsack variant. The direction of one loop changes the mathematical problem. This is the kind of tiny detail that turns your merch bag into an illegal duplication glitch.
Counting has different semantics

Counting combinations, counting ordered sequences, maximizing value, and minimizing cost are different problems. Loop order and initialization matter. If exact weight is required, initialize only zero as reachable; if any weight at most capacity is allowed and values are nonnegative, a best-value array can start at zero. State the contract. Do not copy a template and hope it divines whether order matters.
challenge: One item has weight 2 and value 3; capacity is 4. What goes wrong with upward iteration?
answer: It may produce value 6 by taking the same item twice; the zero-one answer is 3.

title: SEQUENCE DP, LIS, AND INTERVAL DP
hook: The sequel needs a state definition.
beats: Longest increasing subsequence

A subsequence keeps original order but may skip elements. For longest strictly increasing subsequence, define D P at i as the best length ending at i. Try every earlier smaller value to extend it, giving quadratic time. A faster method keeps the smallest possible tail value for each subsequence length and uses lower bound. Those tails summarize possibilities; the tails array itself is not necessarily the actual subsequence.
Grid and sequence alignment

For a grid with right and down moves, each reachable cell receives contributions from above and left. Obstacles block transitions. For longest common subsequence of two strings, a prefix-pair state considers matching final characters or dropping one side. A two dimensional table often costs the product of the input lengths. Rolling rows can save memory when older rows are no longer needed, but reconstruction may require additional information.
Intervals grow by length

Interval dynamic programming solves contiguous subarrays or substrings. Define the answer for a range, then split at a middle point or remove an endpoint. Compute shorter intervals before longer ones. A generic split recurrence often takes cubic time, because there are quadratically many intervals and linearly many split choices. Before optimizing, prove the recurrence and count the states. You cannot speed-run a definition you never wrote.
challenge: In [3,1,2,5,4], give a strictly increasing subsequence of maximum length.
answer: Length 3, for example [1,2,4] or [1,2,5].

title: DAGs, TOPOLOGICAL ORDER, AND CYCLES
hook: The schedule cannot depend on itself.
beats: Dependencies create a directed graph

A directed acyclic graph has directed edges but no directed cycle. A topological order places each prerequisite before the task that depends on it. Compute indegrees, enqueue all zero-indegree vertices, remove them one by one, and decrement outgoing neighbors. If fewer than all vertices are processed, a directed cycle exists. The festival cannot require sound check after the concert and the concert after sound check.
Dynamic programming on a DAG

Process vertices in topological order. For a longest path from a source, initialize that source to zero and other vertices as unreachable. Relax outgoing edges by taking a maximum. For path counts, add contributions instead. Negative edge weights do not break DAG processing because there are no cycles to revisit. The evaluation order guarantees every dependency is ready before its dependent state is finalized.
Do not generalize longest paths blindly

Longest path in a general graph is a very different and often intractable problem when restricted to simple paths. Acyclicity is doing essential work here. For directed cycle detection with DFS, distinguish unvisited, currently active, and finished states; an edge to an active vertex witnesses a cycle. An edge to any previously visited vertex does not always mean a directed cycle.
challenge: Dependencies are A->C and B->C. Name two valid topological orders.
answer: A,B,C and B,A,C. C cannot precede either prerequisite.

title: DIJKSTRA: THE TOUR BUS ROUTER
hook: Shortest path, not shortest-looking path.
beats: Distances improve by relaxation

For nonnegative edge weights, Dijkstra computes shortest distances from a source. Initialize the source to zero and other distances to infinity. Use a min-heap of candidate distance and vertex pairs. Pop the smallest candidate. If it is stale, skip it. Otherwise inspect its outgoing edges and improve a neighbor when current distance plus edge weight is smaller. Push each improvement back into the heap.
Why the next distance is final

When the smallest unsettled distance is selected, no path through a farther unsettled vertex can improve it, because remaining edge weights are nonnegative. That is the core proof. Negative edges invalidate this reasoning. A direct road costing ten may lose to a two-edge route costing two plus three, so BFS by edge count is not enough. We optimize total weight, not number of turns.
Choose the right shortest-path tool

For edges of cost zero or one, zero-one BFS uses a deque. Bellman-Ford handles negative edges and can detect reachable negative cycles, at a higher time cost. Floyd-Warshall computes all-pairs distances in cubic time for small graphs. In Dijkstra, use wide distance types and safe infinity values. A priority queue is a scheduling tool, not permission to overflow while adding a road toll.
challenge: Edges: S->A costs 10, S->B costs 2, B->A costs 3. What is distance to A?
answer: 5, via B. All weights here are nonnegative.

title: DISJOINT SET UNION: MERGE THE FAN CLUBS
hook: We are all in the same group chat now.
beats: Track connected components

Disjoint set union maintains a partition into components. Each element points toward a representative root. Find returns that representative. Unite merges two different components. Path compression shortens future searches, and union by size or rank keeps trees shallow. Together they give extremely small amortized cost, commonly expressed using the inverse Ackermann function. You do not need to evaluate that function to use the structure correctly.
What it answers, and what it does not

DSU is excellent when edges are added and you ask whether two vertices are connected. If their representatives match, they are in the same component. It does not directly provide shortest paths, the actual connecting path, or efficient arbitrary edge deletion. Adding a friendship is easy; deleting one and determining whether the group splits is a different problem. Algorithms do not offer emotional support for free.
Size belongs to the representative

Store component sizes at roots. When merging, attach the smaller tree below the larger and update the new root size. If both vertices already share a root, do nothing. Repeatedly adding the same edge must not inflate the size. Test isolated vertices, redundant unions, and a chain of merges. The companion implementation is tested against a simpler graph connectivity model.
challenge: Unite 0 with 1, then 1 with 2, then 0 with 2. How large is their component?
answer: 3. The final union is redundant and must not increase the size.

title: MINIMUM SPANNING TREES
hook: Connect every stage on a budget.
beats: A different objective from shortest paths

A minimum spanning tree connects every vertex of a connected undirected weighted graph with minimum total edge cost. It is not a shortest-path tree from a source. Kruskal sorts edges by weight and adds an edge whenever its endpoints are in different DSU components. Stop after n minus one chosen edges. If the graph is disconnected, the procedure produces a minimum spanning forest instead.
The cut property explains the choice

Imagine a cut dividing vertices into two groups. A lightest edge crossing that cut can be part of some minimum spanning tree. When Kruskal connects components with a cheapest available edge, an exchange argument can replace a crossing edge in an optimal solution without increasing cost. Ties can create multiple valid minimum trees. The final cost can be unique even when the exact chosen edges are not.
Prim and constraints

Prim grows a tree from a starting vertex, repeatedly adding a cheapest edge leaving the current tree. A heap implementation works well for sparse graphs, while a simple quadratic implementation can suit dense small graphs. Both methods rely on undirected connectivity for the ordinary spanning-tree problem. Do not confuse buying the cheapest network with giving every fan the fastest route home. Those are different budgets and different objectives.
challenge: Triangle edge weights are 2, 3, and 10. What is the MST cost?
answer: 5, using the edges of weights 2 and 3.

title: MODULAR ARITHMETIC AND NUMBER THEORY
hook: Big numbers need a different venue.
beats: Remainders preserve useful operations

When a task asks for an answer modulo M, reduce sums and products appropriately. Normalize negative results with a modulo operation followed by adding M and taking modulo again, provided intermediate arithmetic is safe. Multiplication can overflow before reduction, so use a wide enough type or a suitable modular multiplication technique. The modulus is part of the problem specification; do not invent your favorite prime.
Exponentiation by squaring

To compute a to the b, repeatedly square the base and multiply it into the result when the current exponent bit is one. Halve the exponent each step. This takes logarithmic many multiplications. Under a prime modulus, a nonzero residue has inverse a to the modulus minus two by Fermat's little theorem. More generally, an inverse exists exactly when the value and modulus are coprime. Division modulo M is not ordinary integer division.
GCD, primes, and combinatorics

Euclid's algorithm repeatedly replaces a pair by the second value and the remainder to compute their greatest common divisor. A sieve marks multiples to find primes up to a bound. Factorials and inverse factorials support binomial coefficients under appropriate modulus and range assumptions. Count first, then optimize arithmetic. A number-theory formula without its conditions is a VIP pass printed on a napkin.
challenge: Modulo 7, what is the inverse of 3, and why?
answer: 5, because 3*5 = 15 leaves remainder 1 modulo 7.

title: BITMASKS AND MEET IN THE MIDDLE
hook: Split the search party.
beats: Masks encode small subsets

A bit mask compactly records a subset. Test bit i to ask whether item i is present; set or clear it to change membership. Use a sufficiently wide unsigned or signed type with safe shift bounds. Shifting by the type width or using an overflowing signed shift is not a clever shortcut. A mask gives compact representation, not an automatic escape from the exponential number of subsets.
Subset dynamic programming

For a small set of cities, D P of mask and last city can represent the cheapest path visiting exactly that mask and ending at that city. Extend to an unvisited city. There are roughly two to the n times n states, and transitions can add another factor of n. This can be practical around modest n, but memory becomes serious. Count table entries before announcing your world tour.
Meet in the middle

When n is around forty and direct subset enumeration is too large, split the items into two halves. Enumerate subset sums for each half, then combine them with sorting and binary search or two pointers. Each half has about two to the n over two subsets. For exact target sums, look for target minus each left sum in the right list. The problem did not become polynomial, but the exponent became much more manageable.
challenge: How many subsets per half when 40 items are split evenly?
answer: 2^20 = 1,048,576 per half, versus 2^40 overall.

title: FENWICK TREES: THE DYNAMIC MIXER
hook: Update the track without rebuilding the album.
beats: Dynamic prefix sums

A Fenwick tree supports point additions and prefix-sum queries in logarithmic time, using linear memory. Internally use one-based indices. Each index stores a block whose size is its lowest set bit. To update, repeatedly add that lowest set bit to the index. To query a prefix, repeatedly subtract it while accumulating blocks. Starting an update at zero is a trap because its lowest set bit is zero.
Disjoint blocks cover the prefix

To query the first thirteen positions, the structure can combine a block ending at thirteen, then twelve, then eight. Those blocks cover the requested prefix without overlap. A range sum is the difference of two prefix sums, just as with a static prefix array. The difference is that updates now touch logarithmically many stored blocks rather than forcing a full rebuild.
Compression unlocks more applications

Fenwick trees often pair with coordinate compression to count smaller elements, count inversions, or maintain frequencies. For inversion counting, scan the array and ask how many earlier values exceed the current value. Be precise about equal values: inversions usually require strictly greater. A Fenwick tree is especially natural for additive quantities; more general operations may need different structures or stricter assumptions.
challenge: If [3,1,4,1,5] receives +2 at index 2, what is sum [1,4)?

title: SEGMENT TREES: THE RANGE QUERY STAGE
hook: Every section gets its own manager.
beats: Build summaries of intervals

A segment tree divides an array into intervals. Leaves represent individual values; each internal node combines its two children. For range sum, combine by addition and use zero as the identity. For range minimum, combine by minimum and use positive infinity as the identity. The combine operation must be associative so regrouping does not change the result. It need not always be commutative, so preserve order where required.
Query only useful nodes

A range query ignores disjoint nodes, uses fully covered nodes directly, and splits partially covered nodes. A point update changes one leaf and recomputes ancestors. Standard balanced implementations use linear memory and logarithmic time for these operations. Segment trees are more general than Fenwick trees but also more code to debug. Choose the simplest structure that supports the operations you actually need.
Design the node before coding the tree

For maximum subarray sum, a node can store total sum, best prefix, best suffix, and best subarray. The merge combines information from left and right. Decide whether the empty subarray is allowed, because that changes base values. The interesting algorithm is often the summary and merge rule, not the recursive plumbing. A segment tree cannot rescue a summary that throws away essential information.
challenge: For a range-minimum segment tree, why is zero usually the wrong disjoint identity?
answer: If all actual values are positive, min(actual,0) incorrectly returns zero. Use an appropriately large infinity.

title: LAZY PROPAGATION: DEFER, DO NOT FORGET
hook: Procrastination with a correctness proof.
beats: Updates can cover whole intervals

When a range update fully covers a node, update its summary and record a pending operation instead of descending immediately. For adding x to every element in a segment of length len, its sum increases by x times len. Before later descending into children, push the pending operation to them. Lazy propagation is delayed work with a precise record, not ignoring the email until graduation.
Tags must compose correctly

Two range additions combine by addition. Assignment and addition need more care: a new assignment overrides previous values, while a later addition modifies the assigned value. Operation order matters. Define how a tag acts on a summary, how two tags compose, and what the identity tag is. If these algebraic rules are wrong, a perfectly balanced tree will distribute wrong answers with impressive efficiency.
Test overlapping updates

Test a full-range update followed by a small query, nested updates, disjoint updates, and alternating assignments and additions if supported. Compare against a plain vector on small random cases. This is an advanced extension, not a prerequisite for your first contest. Learn ordinary segment trees and their invariants before adding deferred operations. The sequel should not premiere before the original movie.
challenge: A segment of length 7 has sum 20. Add 3 to every element. New sum?

title: EULER TOURS AND LOWEST COMMON ANCESTORS
hook: Flatten the family tree.
beats: Subtrees become intervals

Run a depth first traversal and record the entry index of each vertex. Place each vertex once in entry order. All vertices in one rooted subtree occupy a contiguous interval from its entry time to its exit boundary. This converts subtree sum queries into array range queries. Combine the flattening with a Fenwick or segment tree for updates. Be clear which Euler-tour convention you use; some tours record vertices multiple times.
Jump by powers of two

Binary lifting stores the ancestor two to the k steps above each vertex. Build the next level by composing two jumps of half that size. To find a lowest common ancestor, first lift the deeper vertex to equal depth. If they differ, lift both from large jumps downward whenever their ancestors differ. Their parents then meet at the lowest common ancestor. Preprocessing uses n log n time and memory; queries are logarithmic.
Paths and further extensions

In an unweighted tree, distance between u and v equals depth u plus depth v minus twice the depth of their lowest common ancestor. Weighted root distances work similarly for path sums. Heavy-light decomposition later breaks paths into a logarithmic number of array intervals. Keep parent, depth, and root conventions consistent. A wrong root ancestor sentinel can turn a family tree into a haunted elevator.
challenge: Depths of u,v,LCA are 5,4,2. What is their unweighted distance?

title: TREE DP AND REROOTING
hook: Every cow wants to be the main character.
beats: A parent summarizes its children

Tree dynamic programming exploits the absence of cycles. For a maximum independent set on a tree, keep two values per vertex: best when selected and best when not selected. If selected, none of its children may be selected. If not selected, each child may choose its better state. Evaluate children before parents. The proof separates independent child subtrees once the parent's state is fixed.
Reroot without recomputing everything

Suppose you want the sum of distances from every vertex to all others in an unweighted tree. First compute subtree sizes and the distance sum from one root. When moving the root across an edge to a child with subtree size s, s vertices become one step closer and n minus s become one step farther. The new answer is old answer plus n minus two s.
Two passes, one invariant

A downward pass gathers subtree information. An outward pass passes the rest-of-tree contribution to each child. More general rerooting may use prefix and suffix combinations of child contributions to exclude one child efficiently. State exactly what information enters and leaves each edge. This is the advanced version of a group project where, miraculously, each member has a defined responsibility.
challenge: n=10 and child subtree size is 7. How does the distance sum change on moving into it?
answer: It decreases by 4: n-2s = 10-14.

title: MONOTONIC STACKS, DEQUES, AND SWEEP LINES
hook: Delete candidates that can never win.
beats: Monotonic stacks

For the next greater element, maintain indices whose values are still waiting for a greater value. When a new value arrives, pop smaller waiting values and resolve their answers. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so total work is linear. Choose strict or non-strict comparisons based on how equal values should behave. Amortized analysis counts the total work across all operations.
Sliding window extrema

A monotonic deque maintains candidate maximum indices for a moving window. Remove expired indices from the front. Remove dominated values from the back before adding the new index. The front then holds the current maximum. A new larger value dominates an older smaller value because it is better and expires later. This proof is stronger than saying the deque seems sorted and therefore probably has good vibes.
Sweep events in order

A sweep line sorts events by position or time and maintains the active state. For interval overlap, starts add activity and ends remove it. Tie handling depends on whether endpoints overlap. For half-open intervals, ending events should stop contributing before starting events at the same coordinate when measuring active count. For area, accumulate active covered length times the distance to the next event. Compression must retain original coordinate gaps.
challenge: For half-open intervals [1,3) and [3,5), what is the maximum overlap?
answer: 1. They touch at a boundary but do not overlap.

title: STRONG COMPONENTS, BRIDGES, AND ARTICULATIONS
hook: Which connection holds the group together?
beats: Mutual reachability

In a directed graph, a strongly connected component is a maximal set of vertices that can all reach each other. Kosaraju uses finishing order and a traversal of the reversed graph; Tarjan uses low-link information and an active stack. Compress each strongly connected component into one vertex, and the resulting condensation graph is a DAG. This can turn a cyclic reachability problem into a dependency problem.
Critical undirected edges

A bridge is an undirected edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. DFS discovery times and low-link values reveal whether a child subtree can reach an ancestor without using its parent edge. If it cannot, that tree edge is a bridge. Articulation vertices similarly disconnect a graph when removed, with a special rule for a DFS root.
Parallel edges matter

In an undirected multigraph, skip the exact parent edge by edge identifier, not every edge to the parent vertex. A second parallel edge provides an alternate route and can prevent an edge from being a bridge. Low-link algorithms are easy to almost understand and almost implement. Trace a triangle, a chain, and a pair of parallel edges before trusting the code. Almost correct is still wrong answer with a confident haircut.
challenge: In a triangle with one extra leaf attached, which edge is a bridge?
answer: Only the edge connecting the leaf to the triangle.

title: OFFLINE QUERIES AND PERSISTENCE
hook: Answer later. Remember earlier.
beats: Offline means all queries are known

If answers do not influence future inputs, you may reorder queries to make them easier. For example, sort queries by a threshold and add eligible items to a data structure as that threshold grows. Restore original answer order using query identifiers. This often replaces repeatedly rebuilding the same state. Offline is about knowing the future input, not disconnecting your Wi-Fi in a dramatic training montage.
Mo's algorithm and rollback

Mo's algorithm reorders static range queries so window endpoints move less overall, provided you can cheaply add and remove an element from the maintained answer. A common bound is roughly n plus q times square root n under standard assumptions. Rollback DSU supports undoing merges; typically avoid path compression because it makes undo bookkeeping harder. Combined with time segmentation, rollback can handle certain offline connectivity problems with deletions.
Persistent versions share unchanged structure

A persistent segment tree keeps earlier versions available. A point update copies only nodes along the changed root-to-leaf path and shares untouched subtrees. Each version has its own root. This supports historical queries and some order-statistics constructions, at logarithmic new nodes per point update. Persistence is not free full copying. The entire idea is to remember history without photocopying the whole universe.
challenge: When is reordering queries unsafe?
answer: When later queries or input values depend on earlier answers, unless another valid transformation handles that dependency.

title: ADVANCED TREE DECOMPOSITIONS
hook: Big trees need smaller conversations.
beats: Heavy-light decomposition

Choose a heavy child based on subtree size and form chains. Any root-to-vertex path crosses only logarithmically many light edges because subtree size shrinks substantially across each one. Flatten chains into an array. A path query becomes a logarithmic number of range queries, commonly giving logarithmic squared time with a segment tree. Direction matters for noncommutative path summaries.
Centroid decomposition

A centroid splits a tree into components of size at most half when removed. Recursively decompose those components. Each vertex participates in logarithmically many centroid levels. This supports some distance-based queries and counting problems when contributions can be combined carefully. Avoid double-counting paths within one child component. The separator is useful because it bounds the recursive depth, not because the word centroid sounds like a robot DJ.
Small-to-large merging

When combining sets or maps from child subtrees, merge the smaller structure into the larger. An element can move only logarithmically many times because its destination size at least doubles each time. The total cost then depends on the underlying container operations. This is another amortized argument. Learn the movement proof; it transfers to many problems beyond trees and helps explain why a deceptively nested algorithm can be efficient.
challenge: Why can an item move only O(log n) times in small-to-large merging?
answer: Each move at least doubles the size of its containing collection, which cannot exceed n.

title: STRING ALGORITHMS: FIND THE HOOK
hook: A repeated chorus is a pattern.
beats: Prefix function and KMP

The prefix function records the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix for each string prefix. When a match fails, reuse a shorter known border instead of restarting blindly. Knuth-Morris-Pratt uses this information to match a pattern in linear total time. The important invariant is how much of the pattern currently matches the text suffix. Borders let you preserve justified progress.
Z values and hashing

The Z function records how much of the whole string's prefix matches at each position. It also supports linear-time pattern work. Polynomial rolling hashes compare substrings quickly after preprocessing, but collisions are possible. Randomized bases or multiple moduli reduce risk; they do not turn hashing into a mathematical guarantee of equality. For a proof that requires exact comparison, use a deterministic method or verify candidates.
Tries, many patterns, and suffix order

A trie stores strings by shared prefixes. Aho-Corasick augments a trie with failure links for matching many patterns. Suffix arrays order suffixes and can combine with longest-common-prefix information for advanced substring questions. These are extensions to study when a problem demands them, not a requirement before solving your first Bronze simulation. Learn what each tool answers before collecting implementations like rare trading cards.
challenge: What is the longest proper prefix of ababa that is also a suffix?
answer: aba, length 3. Proper excludes the entire string itself.

title: FLOW, MATCHING, AND MINIMUM CUTS
hook: How much can the network actually carry?
beats: Capacity limits change the question

A flow network has directed edges with capacities, a source, and a sink. Flow obeys capacity limits and conservation at intermediate vertices. Residual edges represent both unused capacity and the ability to undo earlier choices. An augmenting path increases total flow along a source-to-sink residual path. Reverse residual edges are essential; without them an early routing choice can block a better final solution.
Matching is a useful reduction

In bipartite matching, vertices divide into two groups and edges connect across the groups. Connect a source to the left group with capacity one, each allowed pair with capacity one, and the right group to the sink with capacity one. Maximum flow gives maximum matching. Specialized algorithms can be faster. The reduction works because unit capacities enforce that each endpoint participates in at most one chosen pair.
Cuts certify optimality

The max-flow min-cut theorem says maximum flow equals minimum cut capacity. When no augmenting path remains in an appropriate complete algorithm, reachable residual vertices identify a cut certificate. Dinic combines level graphs with blocking flows; minimum-cost flow adds costs and needs additional care. These are advanced tools with implementation and complexity details worth studying separately. The film gives the model and intuition, not a magic copy-paste license.
challenge: Two fans both want the same single backstage slot. Maximum matching size?
answer: 1, because the slot has capacity one.

title: GEOMETRY, DP OPTIMIZATION, AND THE FRONTIER
hook: There is no final list of every trick.
beats: Geometry starts with exact predicates

The cross product tests orientation of three points and helps build convex hulls. For integer coordinates, use an integer type wide enough for coordinate differences and products. Distinguish collinear from left and right turns. Segment intersection needs endpoint and collinearity cases. Floating-point equality is delicate; choose tolerances only with attention to scale and required accuracy. Draw the degenerate cases, because the judge absolutely will.
Optimization requires structural proofs

Divide-and-conquer DP optimization requires monotonicity of optimal split positions. Knuth optimization has its own stronger recurrence and inequality conditions. Convex hull trick and Li Chao trees optimize queries over lines under specific update and query models. Matrix exponentiation accelerates fixed linear transitions. FFT and NTT accelerate convolution with numerical or modulus constraints. None of these is justified just because the baseline recurrence is slow.
A realistic Platinum extension

Platinum preparation also includes deeper combinatorics, probabilistic reasoning, advanced data structures, and creative combinations of simpler ideas. This chapter is a map of extensions, not a complete course in each. Contest success is not achieved by memorizing a maximum number of algorithm names. It comes from modeling, proving, implementing, testing, and recognizing structure in unfamiliar problems. The final boss is thinking clearly while the clock is being rude.
challenge: What must be checked before applying a DP optimization?
answer: The exact recurrence and the mathematical conditions that justify that optimization, not merely a slow runtime.

title: DEBUGGING: THE BUG HAS NO AURA
hook: Read the evidence. Roast the bug.
beats: Classify the failure

Compilation errors, runtime errors, wrong answers, time limits, and memory limits point to different causes. For a wrong answer, find the smallest failing example and trace state changes. For a crash, check indices, empty containers, invalid iterators, and recursion depth. For time limits, count the actual repeated work. Do not optimize input speed while accidentally running a quadratic algorithm on two hundred thousand elements.
Differential testing

Write a slow reference solver for small inputs. Generate many tiny random cases and compare its answer with the optimized solver. When they differ, save the input and reduce it while preserving failure. Useful invariants include conserved totals, nondecreasing sorted arrays, valid parent relationships, and distances that satisfy every relevant edge inequality. Random testing does not prove correctness, but it is outstanding at exposing unjustified confidence.
Use the compiler as a teammate

Enable warnings during development. Address and undefined-behavior sanitizers can expose memory mistakes and invalid arithmetic operations, though they slow execution and are for local debugging. Test the intended optimized build too. Include one element, duplicates, all equal values, extreme allowed values, disconnected graphs, and adversarial orderings. Your bug does not care that the sample passed. The sample is a sound check, not the whole concert.
code:
g++ -std=c++17 -O1 -g -Wall -Wextra \
    -fsanitize=address,undefined main.cpp -o debug
// Release check:
g++ -std=c++17 -O2 main.cpp -o main
challenge: A fast solver and brute-force solver disagree. What is your next move?
answer: Save and shrink the counterexample, then trace both against the specification; the reference solver can also be wrong.

title: CONTEST STRATEGY: MANAGE THE CLOCK
hook: Do not spend the whole set tuning one string.
beats: Read every problem early

Start by understanding all available problems and their subtasks if present. Choose an entry point where you can make reliable progress. A correct simpler solution can earn useful partial credit when the scoring permits it. Keep time checkpoints so one seductive idea does not consume the whole contest. If stuck, write down the exact missing claim, try a smaller case, or switch problems deliberately.
Submission discipline

Before submitting, verify input and output conventions, indexing, numeric types, complexity, and edge cases. Older practice problems may specify file input and output; current contest instructions may differ. Follow the specific problem and current rules. Remove debugging output. Re-read restrictions on assistance, collaboration, and tools for the contest you enter. This training film is for practice; contest participation must follow the event's rules.
Review is where improvement compounds

After a contest, revisit unsolved problems. Try again before reading an editorial. If you need help, reveal one idea at a time, then close the explanation and implement independently. Re-solve later without notes. Record whether the gap was modeling, proof, implementation, or time management. A score is feedback on one performance, not a measurement of your intelligence. Even Bessie had a debut single called Segmentation Fault.
challenge: After reading an editorial, how do you check that you actually learned the idea?
answer: Explain its invariant and proof, implement from a blank file, and re-solve a related problem later without notes.

title: THE TRAINING ARC: A PLAN THAT SURVIVES MONDAY
hook: Consistency has better stats than panic.
beats: Practice in manageable sessions

A realistic week might include three focused coding sessions, one review session, and occasional timed practice. Adjust that to school, sleep, and enjoyment. Work just beyond current comfort, not five divisions beyond it. Use the official USACO problem archive and a structured resource such as the USACO Guide. These are reference destinations, not claims that every current page or rule has been verified for this film.
Advance by evidence, not a calendar

For C plus plus, independently read input and manipulate vectors safely. For Bronze, solve simulations and small searches with clear reasoning. For Silver, recognize and implement prefix sums, binary search, two pointers, and traversals. For Gold, define DP states and use weighted graphs and dynamic range structures. For Platinum, study selected advanced topics deeply through problems. Promotion timing varies; there is no honest guaranteed schedule.
The parent co-op mode

For a parent, the best question is often: can you show me a tiny example of why this works? Let your son explain and own the keyboard. Celebrate a well-found counterexample and a clear proof, not just a green verdict. If frustration rises, take a break. Turning every evening into a boss fight is how a hobby becomes homework wearing a fake mustache.
challenge: Choose one topic from this film and schedule: learn, solve, review, re-solve.
answer: Example: prefix sums today, two related problems next session, error review afterward, and a blank-file re-solve next week.

title: FINALE: THE PROOF DROPS
hook: Correct. Fast enough. Yours.
beats: The festival finally opens

Bessie's tickets are sorted. Prefix sums handle sales reports. Breadth first search finds exits, Dijkstra routes the bus, and dynamic programming packs the merch. T L E applies for a new job as an hourglass. His resume says extensive experience making people wait. The festival works because every tool has a purpose, every shortcut has a reason, and nobody indexed the secret bonus cow at position n.
The original closing verse

Read the constraints before you chase the crown. Build one small case, write the state down. Prove every move, let the wrong guess go. Test that edge case, then improve the flow. No borrowed voice, no copied track. Just one more problem, and we run it back. If the answer breaks, that is data, not shame. Fix the invariant. Get back in the game.
Your next action

Close the video and write a program from scratch. Start at the earliest chapter where you cannot yet solve the challenge independently. Use the companion workbook, runnable examples, and chapter index to return when needed. This film is your map; the problems are the training. You do not need to know everything today. You need one honest next step, a compiler, and the courage to be temporarily bad at something worth learning.
challenge: Explain one algorithm without naming it. Describe its state, invariant, complexity, and failure conditions.
answer: If you can explain those four things and implement it independently, you are building transferable understanding.
